title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 213: Tapping the Earth's Cauldron: Geothermal Energy
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 213 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

Tapping the Earth's Cauldron: The Geothermal Frontier

Paragraph 1. Iceland is a cold island near the Arctic, yet it gets almost all its electricity and home heat from clean natural sources. Long ago, people imported coal from other countries. Today, Iceland uses underground geothermal energy because hot melted rock, called magma, sits unusually close to the Earth's surface there. Unlike wind or solar power, this underground heat works day and night in every season.

Paragraph 2. How does geothermal power work? First, rainwater falls on volcanic ground and slips deep down through tiny cracks in the rock. When the water reaches hot rock far below, it becomes super hot. Engineers drill deep holes down to one to three kilometres, and the hot water jumps up as strong steam that spins big machines to produce electricity.

Paragraph 3. Geothermal heat is also famous in Reykjavik, Iceland's capital city. Before 1930, people burned smoky coal to heat wooden houses, filling the air with thick black smoke. Then the city built underground pipes to send hot water straight into homes. Today, more than ninety-nine percent of homes in Reykjavik stay warm this way. Extra warm water even flows through plastic pipes under city sidewalks to melt winter snow and ice automatically.

Paragraph 4. Still, deep underground water sometimes holds gases that smell like rotten eggs. At one plant, scientists mix these gases with water and pump them deep into black basalt rock, where the gas turns into solid white stone within two years, keeping the air clean.

groups.title: Questions 1–4
groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

groups.title: Questions 5–8
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

q1.text: Why does Iceland have so much natural heat underground?
options: A. It receives strong tropical sunlight all year.
B. Hot melted rock sits close to the surface there.
C. It imports hot water through pipes from Europe.
D. Its lakes freeze over for nine months every year.

steps: Đoạn 1: Đá nóng chảy (magma) nằm rất gần bề mặt Trái Đất ở Iceland.

q2.text: How is electricity made at geothermal power stations?
options: A. Heavy ocean waves push floating machines near the coast.
B. Rainwater freezes inside pipes to cool down engines.
C. Workers burn volcanic rocks inside large ovens.
D. Strong steam rises up drilled holes to spin machines.

steps: Đoạn 2: Hơi nước mạnh phun lên qua các giếng khoan để làm quay máy phát điện.

q3.text: Why does Reykjavik put warm water pipes under city sidewalks?
options: A. To melt snow and ice automatically in winter
B. To grow fresh vegetables under the streets
C. To prevent rainwater from entering houses
D. To dry wet shoes for people walking outside

steps: Đoạn 3: "...under city sidewalks to melt winter snow and ice automatically."

q4.text: How do scientists stop smelly underground gas from polluting the air?
options: A. By burning the gas in open fields outside town
B. By freezing the gas inside plastic containers
C. By pumping gas-rich water into rock until it turns into stone
D. By sending the gas up tall chimneys into clouds

steps: Đoạn 4: Hòa khí vào nước và bơm xuống đá bazan để nó hóa thành đá trắng cứng.

q5.text: Iceland sells large amounts of geothermal electricity to Norway using undersea cables.

steps: Đoạn 1: Bài không nhắc đến việc xuất khẩu điện sang Na Uy.

q6.text: Before 1930, Reykjavik residents enjoyed clean air without any coal smoke.

steps: Đoạn 3: Trước năm 1930, người dân đốt than đầy khói đen bao phủ thành phố.

q7.text: More than ninety-nine percent of homes in Reykjavik are heated with geothermal water today.

steps: Đoạn 3: "Today, more than ninety-nine percent of homes in Reykjavik stay warm this way."

q8.text: Turning trapped gas into solid stone underground takes over twenty years.

steps: Đoạn 4: Chỉ mất 2 năm (within two years) để hóa đá.
